extracted.intended_audience: judges and patent litigation practitioners (plaintiffs, defendants, in-house counsel), and court case managers
extracted.subtask_description: Best practices and principles for judicial case management of patent litigation, addressing early case management, discovery limits, Markman/claim construction, trial management, jury instructions, experts, eDiscovery, bifurcation, stays/transfers, and exceptional case determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle No. 1 – WG10 is developing these Best Practices to improve the system for resolving patent disputes and make it more fair and efficient.
rubrics_metrics.description: These Best Practices are to apply to and benefit all stakeholders in patent litigation, both bench and bar, and to and for all types of patent holders and accused infringers. They should further the goals of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 1 to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive determination of every action and proceeding, helping ensure a non-frivolous patent litigation system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle No. 2 – Parties should advise the court as soon as practicable whether motions or parallel proceedings are likely to be filed that may substantially affect case management.
rubrics_metrics.description: The court’s case management schedule should require filing of such motions early enough to allow full and fair opportunity to address matters and to facilitate a timely ruling so discovery, motion practice, and trial preparation can be streamlined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle No. 3 – Parties should actively and cooperatively work to narrow asserted claims, representative products, and prior art references in good faith and efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.description: Early narrowing conserves resources and allows the court and parties to focus on the most significant disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle No. 4 – Parties should disclose, formally or informally, the basis for their positions and requests to help the court and parties understand significance.
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing the basis for positions mitigates litigation of issues that are of little significance and helps the court manage discovery and motion practice proportionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle No. 5 – Litigants should file only meritorious motions and oppositions that resolve significant disputes; courts should remedy abuses.
rubrics_metrics.description: Where litigants file non-meritorious or abusive motions (or oppositions), the court should take appropriate action such as awarding fees or granting other relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle No. 6 – Lead counsel should directly manage their litigation strategies from the start and ensure coordination between trial issues and preparation.
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead counsel of both parties should manage strategies and procedures, coordinating what the party intends to try with preparations leading up to trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 1 – The parties should advise the court, no later than the case management conference, on whether a motion for stay is likely.
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclose likelihood of stay motions early so the court can schedule and decide such motions in a way that streamlines subsequent case management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 2 – The parties should advise the court, no later than the case management conference, whether the claims could be stayed against a subset of the defendants (e.g., customers).
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether partial stays may be appropriate so the court can consider segmented management of the litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 3 – The parties should advise the court, no later than the case management conference, whether a motion to transfer is likely.
rubrics_metrics.description: Early notice of anticipated venue/transfer motions allows the court to address and schedule related briefing and decisions to avoid wasted discovery and delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 4 – The plaintiff should promptly identify any pending companion proceedings and any potential coordination or consolidation between them.
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide information on parallel or companion proceedings early so the court can consider coordination, consolidation, or case management accommodations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 5 – The court should encourage parties to work together in good faith to identify representative claims and prior art references early to avoid discovery on all asserted claims and references.
rubrics_metrics.description: If the parties reach an impasse, they should present disputed issues to the court, which should resolve them as soon as practicable to achieve efficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 6 – The court should encourage the patent holder to identify an initial set of representative claims for discovery and claim construction purposes no later than the case management conference.
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties should propose limits on number of representative claims, and the court and parties should decide on a process and timeframe to reach a final limit. Parties should narrow asserted claims during discovery and select final claims for trial at least 30 days prior to service of any expert report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 7 – No later than the case management conference, the alleged infringer should identify the most relevant prior art references it is aware of, and parties should propose positions on limiting references for discovery.
rubrics_metrics.description: At the case management conference, parties and the court should decide on a limit of prior art references to focus discovery and trial preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 8 – The court should encourage the parties, where possible, to work together to identify representative products early to limit accused products that will be the focus of discovery and trial.
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification of representative products promotes efficiency by narrowing discovery and trial scope; if parties cannot agree, the court should resolve disputes promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 9 – The parties should address whether they can agree on representative products for discovery; if not, identify additional information/time needed to reach agreement or a court resolution.
rubrics_metrics.description: If agreement is not reached at the initial case management conference, propose what information and time are necessary to reach a resolution or request court intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 10 – Parties should provide good faith non-binding estimates as to damages range and high-level explanations, as early as possible (at the case management conference).
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing estimated ranges of damages and explanations facilitates proportionality determinations and effective case management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 11 – At the initial case management conference, the court should implement procedures encouraging parties to identify discovery issues needing early resolution.
rubrics_metrics.description: The court should structure the conference to surface likely discovery disputes so they can be addressed proactively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 12 – The court should require disclosures and document production likely to encourage early case resolution.
rubrics_metrics.description: Order or require early disclosure/production of documents that are central to key issues to promote settlement and focused litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 13 – As part of their initial Rule 26(f) conference, parties should attempt to agree to schedules for infringement and invalidity contentions, substantial production of accused-product documents, and for alleged infringer to decide whether to waive privilege and produce opinion letters.
rubrics_metrics.description: Early scheduling of these matters promotes predictability and efficient sequencing of discovery and motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 14 – In the joint case management statement, parties should inform the court how they believe the underlying technology will affect discovery.
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain technology-specific discovery needs so the court can tailor orders (e.g., source code, expert needs, tutorials) appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 15 – At the case management conference, parties should identify any case-dispositive or settlement-driving issues that may warrant focused discovery or early motion practice.
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface early issues (e.g., invalidity, claim construction, venue, IPR impact) so the court can consider expedited motions or tailored discovery to resolve them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 16 – The court should consider implementing different tracks for patent cases, using streamlined discovery and earlier trial dates in appropriate cases.
rubrics_metrics.description: Different tracks enable proportional management tailored to case complexity and resources to promote efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 17 – The court should enter eDiscovery orders outlining the scope and limits of eDiscovery when entering initial case management and protective orders.
rubrics_metrics.description: The order should clarify scope, limits, formats, custodians, search methodologies, and preservation obligations for electronic discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 18 – The court should require the parties know in what form eDiscovery can and will be produced and what limits will exist, as part of its case management order.
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify production formats, metadata, and limits early to avoid disputes and needless burden/cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 19 – The court should require parties to address in the Rule 26 joint discovery plan how and where any computer source code production should be made available to parties and experts.
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify secure review protocols, locations, access limitations, and procedures for source code discovery to protect confidentiality and manage logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 20 – The court should require parties to address whether there should be a patent prosecution bar in the protective order, and the extent such bar should apply to anticipated parallel USPTO proceedings (e.g., IPR).
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether patent prosecution activity should be restricted for those accessing confidential materials and tailor the bar's scope relative to parallel proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 21 – After the case management conference, the court should establish a schedule in a scheduling order that sets dates for claim construction briefing, any related briefing, a tutorial (if any), and a Markman hearing date.
rubrics_metrics.description: Set firm deadlines for claim construction to allow orderly progression to trial and avoid delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 22 – At the case management conference, parties should discuss whether a tutorial prior to the Markman hearing would be beneficial and, if so, the timing, format, and scope.
rubrics_metrics.description: Tutorials can help judges understand technical background; parties should propose logistics and content early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 23 – At the case management conference, the court should inform parties of its preferred format for the Markman hearing.
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide guidance on whether the court prefers live testimony, annexed briefs, witness use, and other logistical aspects of claim construction proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 24 – Should the court wish to utilize a court-appointed expert or technical advisor, raise preference at the initial case management conference or as early as possible.
rubrics_metrics.description: Early notice allows parties to provide input and plan for potential court-appointed technical assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 25 – If the court plans to utilize a court-appointed expert/technical advisor, parties should provide input on candidate selection, and the court should define the individual's role and responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the expert's duties (e.g., advising the court, not advocacy), selection process, and procedural safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 26 – Parties should advise the court, no later than the case management conference, whether a focused claim construction proceeding followed by a limited summary judgment motion is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider staging claim construction with narrow issues followed by targeted summary judgment to resolve dispositive matters early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 27 – The court should identify the dates of the close of fact and expert discovery in a scheduling order soon after a case management conference.
rubrics_metrics.description: Promptly set discovery deadlines to provide certainty and focus for subsequent motion practice and trial preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 28 – The court should consider whether bifurcation of discovery would be appropriate at the case management conference.
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate phasing discovery (e.g., infringement/invalidity separate from damages) to reduce burden and focus disputes efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 29 – The court should address a suitable settlement process at the case management conference.
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider mediation, settlement conferences, or other ADR mechanisms and set timelines to encourage resolution without excessive discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 30 – The court should consider setting the schedule for filing and briefing Daubert motions in a scheduling order following the case management conference, as a distinct deadline separate from and much earlier than motion in limine deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve Daubert challenges well ahead of trial so parties can prepare expert-driven trial strategies in view of rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 31 – The court should set a firm date for the final pretrial conference in a scheduling order following the case management conference.
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixing the final pretrial date provides structure for pretrial exchanges and logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 32 – The court should set a firm trial date in a scheduling order following the case management conference.
rubrics_metrics.description: A firm trial date encourages disciplined discovery and motion practice and aids settlement and case planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 33 – The court should schedule a supplemental case management conference, if warranted, after the initial case management conference.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use supplemental conferences to address emerging issues, refine schedules, or resolve disputes after initial discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 34 – Before the Markman hearing, the court should solicit the parties’ input regarding the length and scheduling of any technology tutorial.
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine tutorial length and scheduling with input so it aids the court without undue burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 35 – The court should inform the parties of its preferences regarding the recording of the tutorial and submission of any materials presented with the tutorial.
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify whether tutorials will be on the record, whether materials become part of the docket, and how they should be handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 36 – The court should instruct the parties to agree on the form of specific terms or phrases submitted for construction or to clarify areas of disagreement.
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage parties to work together to present focused disputed terms and avoid unnecessary proliferation of terms for construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 37 – The parties should prioritize by their relative importance the claim terms to be construed.
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritizing terms helps the court and parties focus resources on the most significant claim construction disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 38 – The court should determine the length of the Markman hearing.
rubrics_metrics.description: Set a hearing length that reflects the number and complexity of contested terms to manage time fairly and efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 39 – If there are a large number of terms to be construed, the court should organize Markman presentations by term, not by parties.
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizing by term reduces redundancy and improves clarity in claim construction proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 40 – Parties proposing 'plain and ordinary meaning' should explain contours of such construction if the term remains ambiguous absent further construction.
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting plain meaning, parties should clarify how that construction resolves ambiguities to aid the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 41 – If parties desire to call witnesses at the Markman hearing, require disclosure of each witness (including CV for experts) and submit a report disclosing opinions to be offered by any expert witness.
rubrics_metrics.description: Advance disclosure of witnesses and expert reports provides the court and opposing parties notice and efficient hearing preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 42 – Daubert motions should generally be decided ahead of trial to facilitate resolution or enable parties to prepare for trial in view of the court’s ruling.
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve Daubert issues early to prevent wasted trial preparation and focus evidentiary disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 43 – The court should limit experts to providing trial testimony only within the scope of their expert reports and require parties to refrain from unwarranted Rule 26 objections.
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforce Rule 26 boundaries to ensure fairness and prevent surprise expert testimony; discourage meritless discovery objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 44 – The court should provide preliminary jury instructions and consider playing for the jury the video 'The Patent Process: An Overview for Jurors.' Typically read instructions and play the video after jury selection.
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary instructions and educational materials help jurors understand patent basics and improve comprehension during trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 45 – The court should consider permitting juror notebooks and allowing jurors to take notes.
rubrics_metrics.description: Note-taking and notebooks can help jurors track issues and evidence, improving engagement and deliberation quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 46 – The court should consider allowing juror questions, which can enhance engagement and understanding, but be careful they do not become time-consuming or create juror bias.
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow juror questions with safeguards to balance engagement and efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 47 – The court should permit brief interim statements, such as witness introductions.
rubrics_metrics.description: Short interim statements can assist juror orientation without disrupting witness examination or creating prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 48 – In longer patent trials, the court should consider allowing some interim arguments.
rubrics_metrics.description: Interim arguments can help clarify issues for jurors during lengthy trials if managed to avoid undue delay or bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 49 – At the final pretrial conference, the court should set time limits for trial.
rubrics_metrics.description: Impose reasonable time limits to ensure efficient presentation and to prevent undue delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 50 – At the final pretrial conference, the court should limit the number of exhibits and encourage demonstratives and summaries under Rule 1006.
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit exhibits and promote demonstratives/summaries to streamline trial and reduce juror confusion and time spent handling voluminous documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 51 – The court should consider pre-admitting exhibits to allow trial to flow without objections and time spent admitting exhibits one-by-one.
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-admission of agreed exhibits saves trial time and reduces evidentiary disputes during trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 52 – At the final pretrial conference, the court should consider whether bifurcation of certain issues or claims will expedite trial and promote the jury’s ability to digest the facts of the case.
rubrics_metrics.description: Bifurcation (e.g., liability first, damages later) can simplify jury work and allow efficient resolution of discrete issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 53 – The court should rule on the objective prong for willfulness before trial if the conclusion is obvious and clear.
rubrics_metrics.description: If the objective prong (e.g., objective recklessness) is clearly answered as a matter of law, decide it pretrial to narrow issues for trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 54 – The court should hear and weigh all evidence of willfulness during the jury trial in significantly contested cases.
rubrics_metrics.description: In contested willfulness disputes, present evidence to the jury for consideration rather than depriving them of contested facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 55 – Each verdict form question should include a citation to the jury instruction corresponding to that question.
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite the applicable instruction for each verdict question to avoid confusion and ensure consistency between instructions and verdict form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 56 – The parties should consider having each verdict form question include the applicable burden of proof.
rubrics_metrics.description: Including burdens of proof on the verdict form helps jurors apply correct standards when answering questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 57 – Verdict forms should include questions as to whether the court is submitting only underlying factual questions to the jury, with instructions explaining the court's responsibility for legal determinations.
rubrics_metrics.description: If the court is submitting only factual predicates (with the court making legal conclusions), explain to the jury why that is done to avoid confusion about their role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 63 – The jury instructions should identify the burden of proof required to make a showing of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the court submits obviousness to the jury, the instructions may state that the alleged infringer must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the claimed invention was obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 64 – The jury instructions should describe the relevant factors involved in the obviousness determination in some detail depending upon nature and scope of disputes between parties.
rubrics_metrics.description: Only disputed factual issues need instruction; describe relevant factors (e.g., level of ordinary skill, differences between claimed invention and prior art) in adequate detail to allow jurors to appreciate their import.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 65 – Jury instructions should specifically identify each prior art reference or combination being asserted to invalidate each claim under obviousness and the details of the dispute.
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent possible, submit only a limited number of asserted combinations to the jury and provide guidance on what constitutes pertinent or analogous art; highlight preliminary factual disputes (e.g., availability dates) that must be resolved first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 66 – For level of ordinary skill in the art, jury instructions should provide guidance on factors that can be considered (education, experience, problems encountered, sophistication of technology).
rubrics_metrics.description: List factors such as levels of education/experience, types of problems encountered, and the sophistication of technology to help jurors assess level of skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 67 – Parties should try to agree on relevant differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; instructions should provide guidance on comparing differences in context of the invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize that inventions are typically combinations of prior art building blocks and comparisons should be from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill, avoiding reliance on the patent itself (no hindsight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 68 – Jury instructions should briefly describe each secondary consideration in dispute, grouping factors that show obviousness and those that show nonobviousness; highlight need for sufficient nexus and that no factor alone is dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain commercial success, copying, long-felt need, unexpected results, and caution jurors about common mistakes (e.g., attributing commercial success to marketing rather than invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 69 – If the verdict form contains separate questions on each obviousness factor, instructions should make clear connection between the instructions and the corresponding question(s).
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize instructions in same structure as verdict form with section and paragraph numbers corresponding to verdict questions and ideally provide jurors copies during deliberations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practice 70 – Where the court submits the ultimate determination of obviousness to the jury, the jury instructions should provide guidance on how that determination should be made.
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide explanations of terms and the balance between patentable invention and application of common sense; warn against hindsight; list specific questions jurors may consider (reasons to combine, known techniques, whether it was 'obvious to try').

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional Case Determinations – Considerations following Octane Fitness and Highmark regarding §285 attorney’s fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Issues include whether/when to plead requests for an exceptional case determination; what discovery to allow and when; timing of motions; what evidence courts should consider for §285; whether partial exceptional determinations are appropriate; whether exceptional status may be tied to specific points in litigation; and whether success or contingency fees are recoverable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working Group 10 is developing further Best Practices on these topics and will publish them separately for public comment.
